title: Random domain decomposition for parabolic PDEs on graphs: the convergence theorem (Theorem 2.3)
author: Mart\'in Hern\'andez
work: Random domain decomposition for parabolic PDEs on graphs
difficulty_reason:
Counted unit: the paper's convergence theorem for the continuous random batch method, printed as Theorem 2.3 of the paper (source0.tex lines 331--337; the environment carries the optional title Convergence and the source label th:convergence), delivered together with the paper's own complete proof of it at source0.tex lines 675--1128. The statement is that for the parabolic problem on the graph, its random-batch approximation and the randomized coefficients, the quantity Lambda measuring the variance of the randomization is uniformly bounded in the batch step size and the mean-square error between the two solutions is bounded, uniformly in time, by a constant times the square root of the L1 norm of Lambda times the step size h, with a constant independent of h. It is the paper's main result: the abstract advertises exactly this first-order mean-square convergence of the random batch method at the level of the partial differential equation, without any preliminary discretization in space or time.

The author's proof is complete and extends over roughly four hundred and fifty lines of the source. The author forms the difference of the two solutions, differentiates its squared L2 norm on each randomization interval, decomposes the resulting bilinear expression into the four groups of terms produced by the randomized coefficients, the randomized source and the randomized interval selection, and estimates each group separately: the leading terms are absorbed into the unperturbed energy identity, the remaining ones are bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz, by the boundedness of the coefficients and by the definition of Lambda, and the sums over the random batches are replaced by their expectations using the exchangeability of the batches. The resulting differential inequality is closed by Gronwall's lemma, which produces a bound with an exponential factor in the final time, and the last step converts the surviving double integral of the time derivative of the random solution into a single factor of the step size by first proving an absolute-continuity estimate for the random solution, and then invokes the energy estimate of the paper's well-posedness theorem for the random system to bound the remaining norm by a constant that is independent of h. The proof therefore depends on the paper's own maximal-regularity theorem, on the well-posedness theorem for the random system, on the boundedness lemma for Lambda, and on the whole machinery of the randomized decomposition, all of which are retained in the delivered document.

Carrying this out requires, beyond the standard energy method for parabolic problems, the randomization of a domain decomposition with a non-overlapping cover of the graph, the correct splitting of the consistency error into the terms that can be absorbed and the terms that must be paid for by Lambda, the interchange of the expectation with the time integral over a random number of intervals, and the careful tracking of the constants so that none of them depends on the step size. No qualifying examination poses this: the argument is the technical core of a research paper on random domain decomposition for partial differential equations on graphs, it is stated for a general graph with piecewise smooth coefficients and boundary data, and the constant is required to be uniform in the batch step size. That places the unit in the research range: H3.
